content.definition: That part of the nerve head visible with the ophthalmoscope is termed the optic disc. Its intrapapillary parts are the optic cup and the neuroretinal rim, which are separated, by the scleral ring of Elschnig, from a zone of parapapillary atrophy variably present on the temporal side; the scleral ring represents the border tissue of the nerve. Disc, cup and rim areas or diameters and vessel width do not correlate with age after the age of 10 to 15 years, or with sex, or side, in eyes with refractive errors within the range of plus or minus 5 dioptres (p. 505). The pink colour of the disc is due to the rich capillary supply to its rim, demonstrable by fluorescein angiography and most noticeable inferotemporally where the rim is widest; the white appearance of the cup is due to scattering of light by the lamina cribrosa and the sparse vascularity of this region, the unmyellinated and relatively transparent axons themselves scattering little light (p. 505).
content.location: The disc corresponds in size to the internal opening of the scleral canal. The scleral canal is bounded by the border tissue which separates nerve fibres from choroid and sclera, is about 0.5 mm in length, and may be straight or directed slightly nasally, temporally or downwards; three shapes are recognizable — a cone narrowest at the basal lamina; narrowing to the inner third of the sclera and uniform beyond this; and hourglass-shaped with a waist in the intermediate third of the sclera. In the first two shapes a scleral ring is present, visible by ophthalmoscopy (p. 505). The foveola lies 0.53 (plus or minus 0.34) mm below the optic disc centre (p. 506), and the retinal vessels emerge on the medial side of the cup, slightly decentred superonasally (pp. 507-508).
layers: Surface nerve fibre layer: the unmyelinated axons converge on the disc; the layer is most visible inferotemporally, then superiorly, then supero- and inferonasally (Jonas et al., 1989d), correlating with the configuration of the neuroretinal rim (broadest inferiorly then superiorly) and the juxtapapillary calibres of the retinal vessels (widest inferotemporally, then superotemporally, then supero- and inferonasally — Jonas and Schiro, 1993); thickness and visibility decrease with age with the loss of about 4-5000 axons per year (Jonas and Naumann, 1991), and axonal loss in experimental glaucoma involves apoptosis at least in part (Quigley, 1995) (p. 508).

Prelaminar zone: the neural part of the nerve head anterior to the lamina, its axons surrounded by astrocytic glia; supplied mainly from the scleral short posterior ciliary system and recurrent choroidal arteries (see optic_nerve_blood_supply) (pp. 528, 531, 534).

Laminar zone (lamina cribrosa): the fenestrated connective-tissue plates through which the axon bundles pass; the area of the lamina averaged 2.88 (plus or minus 0.84) mm2 and ranged from 1.62 to 5.62 mm2 (ratio 1:3.5), independent of age over 15 years, sex and side; the pore count on the inner surface averaged 227 (plus or minus 36, range 168-292) and increases with lamina area; the mean single pore area (0.00387 plus or minus 0.00091 mm2) and total pore area are larger in the inferior and superior regions than in the temporal regions and greater in the peripheral part of the lamina (Jonas, Fernandez and Naumann, 1991) (p. 506).
Retrolaminar zone: the myelinated axons behind the lamina cribrosa, invested in dural, arachnoid and pial sheaths (p. 499).
content.blood_supply: The optic nerve head is a watershed zone between the retina and the optic nerve, whose vessels are exposed to significantly different hydrostatic pressures — the disc and retina to intraocular pressure, the retrolaminar and proximal nerve to cerebrospinal fluid pressure (p. 528). Excluding the superficial nerve fibre layer, the disc and retrolaminar nerve receive their blood supply mainly, if not entirely, from the short posterior ciliary artery system, with major variation between individual nerve heads (p. 528). Retrolaminar region: supply chiefly from the arteries and arterioles of the pial sheath of the neighbouring leptomeninges; recurrent scleral short posterior ciliary arteries supply the arterioles at the meningoscleral interface — the circles of Zinn and Haller, found infrequently by some authors (Hayreh, 1974) but commonly present and an important supply to both retrolaminar and laminar parts per more recent studies (Olver et al., 1990); some choroidal arteries also supply the retrolaminar region (Hayreh, 1975; Anderson and Braverman, 1976); the central retinal artery gives a small number of intraneural branches whose contribution is small relative to the pial supply (p. 529). Laminar region: the anastomotic circles of Zinn (1755) and Haller (1754) are formed by the paraoptic branches of the short posterior ciliary arteries; their branches are (1) recurrent pial branches — four to seven from each segment or from two or three larger trunks; (2) recurrent choroidal branches supplying the immediate peripapillary choroid, whose small centripetal branches supply the laminar and retrolaminar regions; (3) direct branches to the retrolaminar and laminar parts, relatively infrequent; (4) arteriole-arteriolar anastomoses between the circle and pial and recurrent choroidal arterioles. Interfacial precapillaries within the glial border tissue (Ruskell, 1984) are thin-walled and vulnerable to raised intraocular pressure, possibly related to the disc haemorrhages of chronic glaucoma (p. 531). Prelaminar region: supplied mainly from the scleral short posterior ciliary system — branches course through the sclera and the border tissue of Elschnig to reach the prelaminar space without traversing the choroid (Lieberman, Maumenee and Green, 1976) — and the recurrent choroidal arteries, although Lieberman et al. (1976) found that only 10% of vessels entering the prelaminar region originate from choroidal arteries although about 30% of the prelaminar depth is in contact with peripapillary choroid; a microvascular cuff is present between disc and choroid immediately external to the peripapillary bundle of optic nerve axons, regarded as the anterior extension of the pial vascular bed (p. 534). Superficial nerve fibre layer: the central retinal artery is the major supply, through (1) peripapillary arterioles of central retinal artery origin, (2) epipapillary arterioles of central retinal artery origin, (3) rich anastomoses with the prelaminar region, (4) occasional anastomoses with the choriocapillaris, and (5) precapillary branches from cilioretinal arteries when present; peripapillary arterioles are more important than epipapillary (Anderson and Hoyt, 1969; Hayreh, 1974), with rich anastomoses to the radial peripapillary network (Michaelson and Campbell, 1940; Toussaint, Kuwabara and Cogan, 1961; Henkind, 1967) (p. 534). The temporal part of the laminar region is much more vascular than the remainder (p. 534).
content.venous_drainage: The venous drainage of the optic nerve head is much simpler than its arterial supply: in each zone venules drain into the central retinal vein, or when present into a duplicated vein (probably an embryological persistence of hyaloid veins — Hayreh, 1963). Occasional septal veins in the retrolaminar region drain into pial veins; some small venules from the prelaminar region or from the nerve fibre layer (opticociliary veins) drain into the choroid (Lieberman, Maumenee and Green, 1976) and may enlarge in association with optic nerve sheath meningiomas (p. 534).
content.histology_summary: Disc size: normal disc area ranges widely, from 0.86 mm2 to 5.54 mm2 with a mean of 2.69 (plus or minus 0.7) mm2 (Jonas, Gusek and Naumann, 1988) (Table 15.1); primary macrodiscs, of areas more than two standard deviations above the mean (greater than 4.09 mm2), may be associated with pits of the optic nerve and 'Morning Glory' syndrome, and microdiscs (less than 1.29 mm2) were identified at the other extreme (Jonas and Naumann, 1991); secondary macrodiscs accompany the acquired globe enlargement of high myopia and buphthalmos and may reach 20 mm2. A side difference in area of 0.1 mm2 or less occurs in 28% of normal subjects, of 0.2 mm2 or less in 46% and of 0.5 mm2 or less in 84% (p. 505). Disc width (Table 15.1, Jonas, Gusek and Naumann, 1988): horizontal 1.76 (plus or minus 0.31) mm (0.91-2.61), vertical 1.92 (plus or minus 0.29) mm (0.96-2.91); cup area 0.72 (plus or minus 0.70) mm2 (0.0-3.41); cup diameter horizontal 0.92 (plus or minus 0.48) mm, vertical 0.84 (plus or minus 0.47) mm; cup volume median 0.279 mm3, average 0.342 mm3, and cup depth median 0.214 mm, average 0.236 mm (Rohrschneider et al., 1994); rim area 1.97 (plus or minus 0.50) mm2 (0.80-4.66); cup/disc ratio horizontal 0.51 (plus or minus 0.23), vertical 0.43 (plus or minus 0.21). Disc shape: usually oval, the vertical diameter being on average 9% longer than the horizontal, while the cup is 8% wider in the horizontal, so that the rim is wider above and below (p. 505). Optic cup: a funnel-shaped depression usually off-centre towards the temporal side; cup area correlates with disc area; the cup was absent in one-third of the discs of Jonas, Gusek and Naumann (1988), such discs being smaller than average; cups were found shallow in 23%, of medium depth in 31% and deep in 25% (Witusek, 1966); using the direct ophthalmoscope the cup was present in 72% (Ford and Sarwar, 1963) to 78% (Witusek, 1966) of subjects, more commonly in emmetropes (86%) than in hypermetropes (34%) or myopes (5%) (Bednarski, 1925); the cup tends to be larger in discs with steep, punched-out cups (1.37 plus or minus 0.62 mm2) than in those with flat temporal slopes (0.59 plus or minus 0.39 mm2); three-dimensional confocal studies found median cup volume 0.28 mm3 and median cup depth 0.63 mm in normal subjects (Rohrschneider et al., 1994) (p. 506). Neuroretinal rim: contains the retinal nerve axons entering the nerve head; rim area correlates with disc area; it is broadest in the lower segment of the disc, then above, then nasally and then temporally, and is narrowest in the temporal horizontal disc region in 99.2% of all discs — a configuration correlating with the larger retinal vessel calibres below and temporal, better nerve fibre visibility in the inferior temporal arcade, and the foveola lying below the disc centre, implying a greater retinal axonal mass and vascularity in the inferotemporal sector; inter-eye rim area differences of 0.1 mm2 or less occur in 31% of normals, 0.2 mm2 or less in 52% and 0.5 mm2 or less in 84%; rim area is not correlated with ametropia (plus or minus 5 dioptres), sex or side (pp. 506-507). Cup/disc ratio: median value 0.3; it does not differ by more than 0.1 between the two eyes in 92% of subjects or by more than 0.2 in 99%; the vertical ratio is normally lower than the horizontal in 93.2% of normals (p. 507). Parapapillary chorioretinal atrophy: two zones are described, both usually at the temporal margin of the disc (Jonas et al., 1989a, 1989b; Jonas, Fernandez and Naumann, 1992b), corresponding to the older choroidal and scleral crescents of Hogan, Alvarado and Weddell (1971); zone alpha, the more peripheral, is an irregular hypo- or hyperpigmented region with histological irregularities of the retinal pigment epithelium and parapapillary choroid (the choroidal crescent); zone beta, related to the disc centrally, consists of marked atrophy of the pigment epithelium and choriocapillaris with good visibility of the larger choroidal vessels (the scleral crescent), always closer to the disc than zone alpha; in the normal nerve head zone alpha is significantly larger and more frequent (83.9%) than zone beta (16.3%) (Table 15.1 frequencies 84.4% and 15.2%; areas 0.41 plus or minus 0.37 mm2 and 0.13 plus or minus 0.42 mm2); both zones are largest in the temporal horizontal meridian; zone alpha contributes a relative scotoma and zone beta an absolute scotoma to the blind spot (Jonas, Fernandez and Naumann, 1991) (p. 507). Vessels: the diameter of the inferior temporal parapapillary vessels is larger than the superior, corresponding to the broader inferior disc and the greater nerve fibre visibility below; venous pulsation is observed at the disc in 15-90% of normal subjects (Hedges et al., 1994); retinal photoreceptor count, surface area and optic disc size are correlated in normal eyes with axial length shorter than 26 mm (Panda-Jonas et al., 1994) (p. 508).
content.clinical_importance: Certain morphological features of the disc may predispose to optic nerve head disease: small optic discs have a smaller number of optic nerve fibres than large discs and a smaller scleral canal; non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy is commoner in smaller optic nerve heads, due to problems of vascular perfusion and limited space, and optic nerve head drusen and pseudopapilloedema are also encountered with smaller (particularly highly hypermetropic) discs (pp. 505-506). In primary open angle and other chronic glaucomas a progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells produces a characteristic pattern of axonal loss at the neuroretinal rim with cup enlargement, particularly at the upper and lower poles; the vertically-oval cup of chronic glaucoma contrasts with the horizontally-oval cup of the normal disc; flame-shaped haemorrhages on the rim, usually at the inferior or superior temporal margin, are an early sign of glaucoma rarely seen in normal eyes (p. 507). The cup/disc ratio has a median value of 0.3, and an inter-eye asymmetry of greater than 0.2 is taken to signify enlargement and to be of diagnostic importance in glaucoma; a vertical cup/disc ratio of 0.4 or less is often taken to imply the absence of glaucoma, but disc size must be taken into account — since small discs commonly have no cup, a cup/disc ratio of 0.2-0.3 in a small disc may in fact indicate early glaucomatous damage, whereas in a primary macrodisc a ratio of 0.8 may be entirely normal (p. 507). Rim loss occurs in regions furthest from the central retinal trunk (Jonas and Fernandez, 1994), and the susceptibility of the superior and inferior disc regions to damage may be associated with the higher pore-to-disc area in these regions (Quigley and Addicks, 1981; Radius, 1981) (p. 506). In primary open angle glaucoma the area of zone alpha averages 0.65 (plus or minus 0.49) mm2 compared to 0.4 (plus or minus 0.32) mm2 in normal subjects, and zone beta averages 0.79 (plus or minus 1.17) mm2 compared to 0.13 (plus or minus 0.42) mm2, zone beta being found significantly more frequently; however, advanced glaucomatous atrophy may occur without abnormal parapapillary atrophy, and atrophy may surround the disc in the absence of glaucoma (p. 507).
